propositions.text: Claimants are Afghan citizens seeking protection under Sections 96 and 97 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX and the person whom she alleges is her son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, the minor claimant, are citizens of Afghanistan. They claim protection under Sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The applicant claims protection under Sections 96 and 97 of IRPA as Afghan citizens, including a minor alleged son.

propositions.text: Claimant is from Kabul, was a XXXX, husband worked on XXXX projects, and husband received Taliban threats in 2011.
propositions.quote: The claimant is from Kabul. She was a XXXX, and her husband worked XXXX XXXX XXXX projects. On XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, 2011 her husband received threatening phone calls from the local well-known Taliban Commander XXXX to leave their jobs with the puppet government.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states she is from Kabul, was a XXXX, and her husband received Taliban threats in 2011.

propositions.text: In 2011 husband contacted smuggler to come to Canada, disappeared after visiting brothers in 2012, believed kidnapped by Taliban commander.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 they moved and her husband spoke to a smuggler about coming to Canada. In XXXX 2012, he went to visit his brothers to get more money from land sales, but he never came back. She believes he was taken by Commander XXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant reported husband's disappearance to Kabul police but was told to report to another province; she did not report due to planned departure.
propositions.quote: She went to the police in Kabul but they said to report to XXXX province, but she did not because they were scheduled to leave.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant says husband disappeared in 2012, believed kidnapped, and police advised reporting elsewhere but she did not due to leaving.

propositions.text: Claimants are not Convention refugees under Section 96 due to lack of well-founded fear on Convention grounds.
propositions.quote: The Panel finds the claimants not to be Convention refugees under Section 96,2 as they do not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Afghanistan on any of the five Convention grounds.

propositions.text: Claimants are not persons in need of protection under Section 97 as removal would not pose personal risk to life or cruel treatment.
propositions.quote: The Panel also finds that the claimants are not persons in need of protection under section 97,3 as, on a balance of probabilities, their removal to Afghanistan would not subject them personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

propositions.text: Panel's reasons for findings follow.
propositions.quote: The Panel's reasons are as follows.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimants not refugees or in need of protection under Sections 96 and 97, giving reasons next.

propositions.text: Claimant gave most oral testimony; minor claimant questioned at hearing end.
propositions.quote: The claimant gave the great majority of the oral testimony. Counsel questioned the minor claimant at the end of the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notes claimant gave most testimony; minor questioned at hearing end.

propositions.text: Panel considered identity, credibility, well-founded fear, risk to life, and all evidence and submissions.
propositions.quote: The Panel considered the issues of identity, credibility and the well-foundedness of the claimants' alleged fear of persecution, risk to life, etc., i.e., objective basis. The Panel considered all the evidence as well as counsel's oral submission at the close of the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker considered identity, credibility, fear, risk, evidence, and submissions.

propositions.text: Claimants are Afghan citizens per passports but claimant failed to prove husband is minor's father or that they are mother and son.
propositions.quote: The Panel accepts that the claimants are citizens of Afghanistan, from the copies of their Afghani passports supplied... the Panel does not necessarily accept that the claimant was married to her alleged husband, nor that the claimants are indeed mother and son.

propositions.text: No marriage or birth certificates provided; names differ; claimant's age at birth inconsistent; claimants not mother and son.
propositions.quote: The claimant could supply no marriage certificate nor birth certificate for the minor... All the factors lead the Panel to find that the claimants are not mother and son.

propositions.text: Neither counsel nor claimant requested post-hearing time to provide missing documents.
propositions.quote: The Panel notes at this time that neither counsel nor claimant requested time, post-hearing, to provide further documents, missing as of the hearing, which might have assisted their claim.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimants are Afghan citizens but rejects mother-son relationship due to lack of documents and inconsistencies.

propositions.text: Claimant could not document route to Canada or presence in Afghanistan after 2011; arrival date in Canada unknown.
propositions.quote: The claimant could not document any part of their alleged route to Canada, nor that they were even in Afghanistan at any time after XXXX 2011... it is impossible to document when they arrived.

propositions.text: Possible claimants were outside Afghanistan later in 2011; full analysis of prior claims or delays impossible.
propositions.quote: Thus, it is possible the claimants were somewhere else than Afghanistan later in 2011... the Panel may have been deprived of the ability to conduct a full analysis of issues such as failure to, and previous claim, elsewhere, and delay in claiming in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant failed to document route or presence in Afghanistan after 2011, hindering full analysis.

propositions.text: Claimant's document purporting to confirm she was a XXXX is not genuine; admitted tampering with government document.
propositions.quote: The claimant admitted that she, or those for whom she is responsible, tampered with an alleged Government document, and presented it to the Board with no explanation or notation that this had been done.

propositions.text: Submission of false document leads to negative credibility inference; document given no weight; claimant not a XXXX.
propositions.quote: From the submission of a false document the panel is entitled to make a general negative inference as to credibility, and it does so... the Panel finds that she was not a XXXX as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's document false, leading to negative credibility and rejection of XXXX status claim.

propositions.text: Claimant's husband's employment inconsistent; job letter shows different occupation; negative credibility inference made.
propositions.quote: The job letter in Exhibit C-11 indicates that he was a XXXX XXXX XXXX which the Panel finds to be quite different from XXXX... the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

propositions.text: Job letter given little weight; claimant's husband not employed as alleged.
propositions.quote: ...further affords the job letter little weight, and thus finds that the claimant was not employed by the "XXXX" as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds husband's employment claims inconsistent and not credible, giving little weight to job letter.

propositions.text: Claimant could not document Taliban commander's existence or role; night letters not signed or mentioning him; no police report.
propositions.quote: However, she could in no way document that this man exists, or existed, or had the alleged role in the Taliban... neither of these is signed by, or mentions, this man... no police report.

propositions.text: Claimant did not complain to police about night letters; omission from PIF is serious and negative credibility inference made.
propositions.quote: The claimant did not complain to the police about them... the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant testified husband reported night letters to police but did not mention this in Narrative; no police report exists.
propositions.quote: Further, the claimant testified that in fact her husband did report the night letters to the police, when she had not mentioned this in her Narrative, and of course there is no police report.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant failed to document Taliban commander or night letters, with omissions harming credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant's testimony on threat calls inconsistent with Narrative; omission unexplained; negative credibility inference made.
propositions.quote: When asked why she failed to testify as to what she had written in her Narrative... She said she might have missed that. However, the Panel does not accept this explanation... panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's inconsistent testimony on threat calls unexplained, harming credibility.

propositions.text: Night letter about girls' schooling not addressed to claimant; claimant's explanation rejected due to XXXX status rejection.
propositions.quote: One of the night letters referred to not sending girls to school... the Panel does not accept this explanation.

propositions.text: Night letters found not genuine; threat calls did not occur.
propositions.quote: As a result of all the above... the Panel finds that the night letters are not genuine, and that the three alleged threat calls did not actually occur.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker rejects claimant's explanation for night letters and finds letters and threat calls not genuine.

propositions.text: Claimant's testimony on quitting job inconsistent with PIF dates; explanations not accepted; negative credibility inference made.
propositions.quote: She was asked why she had indicated in her PIF that she left her job in XXXX 2011... The Panel does not accept the claimant's explanations... panel makes negative inferences as to credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's inconsistent testimony on job quitting dates not credible.

propositions.text: Claimant's husband's alleged kidnapping unsubstantiated; no police or media reports exist.
propositions.quote: The Panel also does not accept that the claimant's husband was kidnapped as alleged... there is no police report, missing person's report, media article, etc.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds husband's alleged kidnapping unsubstantiated due to lack of reports.

propositions.text: Overall claimant's evidence not credible and insufficient to support refugee protection claim.
propositions.quote: As indicated above, from all the above credibility concerns, the Panel finds the claimant's evidence to be, overall, not credible, and thus insufficient to support her claim for refugee protection

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's evidence overall not credible and insufficient for refugee protection.

propositions.text: Minor's testimony about father's kidnapping and mother's risk rejected as those allegations were rejected.
propositions.quote: The minor said his father was kidnapped, and his mother is at risk for being a XXXX, therefore he is at risk. However, as these allegations have been thoroughly rejected above, the Panel does not accept this argument of the minor.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker rejects minor's testimony relying on rejected allegations.

propositions.text: Minor's age inconsistency raises identity and credibility doubts.
propositions.quote: The minor first said he was 17, which is a concern to the Panel in regard to identity... the Panel notes, a teenager would easily be expected to know at least how old he is.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker doubts minor's credibility due to inconsistent age testimony.

propositions.text: Allegation of minor's fear of forced recruitment added late without explanation; negative credibility inference made.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked why there was an allegation, only at the very end of the hearing, that there is a fear on behalf of the minor of forced recruitment by the Taliban... She could provide no explanation, thus the Panel finds even the addition of this alleged head of fear to be an embellishment at the hearing, from which the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds late addition of minor's fear allegation unexplained and not credible.

propositions.text: Claimant is female and may face risk in Afghanistan without male protection, but claimant's husband status not accepted, so no persecution found.
propositions.quote: However, it is evident the claimant is female... the Panel cannot even accept that the claimant would be without a husband if she hypothetically returned to Afghanistan, thus the Panel finds that the claimant would not be subject to persecution for this reason.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds no persecution risk for claimant as female given doubts about husband's absence.

propositions.text: The Panel considered the general situation of women in Afghanistan regarding Taliban targeting.
propositions.quote: The Panel has also considered the situation of women in general in Afghanistan.

propositions.text: It is hypothetically possible Taliban could target females for kidnapping or dress code violations.
propositions.quote: It is hypothetically possible that the Taliban could target any females in Afghanistan, for kidnapping or even for not dressing in a fully Islamic fashion.

propositions.text: No past allegations or convincing evidence show significant deterioration since 2011 when claimants left.
propositions.quote: There was no allegation that this has happened in the past, nor any convincing evidence that the situation has deteriorated significantly since 2011 when the claimants left Afghanistan.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence shows the female claimant is more likely targeted than other Afghan females.
propositions.quote: no persuasive evidence or argument has been adduced, nor is the Panel aware of any, that would make the female claimant more of a hypothetical target of the Taliban or other such potential agents of persecution than any other female Afghans.

propositions.text: No allegation family is high profile or politically opposed to Taliban or government.
propositions.quote: There was not any allegation that the family is of particularly high profile that would attract the attention of the Taliban or others, and, it is recalled, the allegations that the claimant was a XXXX and her husband worked for "XXXX" were rejected. No evidence was submitted that the family publicly expressed any political opinion opposed to the Taliban, or for the West of the Government.

propositions.text: Taliban could hypothetically target anyone, but no evidence shows claimants are more likely targets than others.
propositions.quote: It is hypothetically possible that the Taliban could target anyone in Afghanistan. However, no persuasive evidence or argument has been adduced, nor is the Panel aware of any, that would make either of the claimants more of a hypothetical target of the Taliban than any other Afghans.

propositions.text: Minor could be kidnapped for forced recruitment, but evidence shows only a mere possibility, not serious likelihood of persecution.
propositions.quote: In this regard, it is conceivably possible that the minor could be kidnapped by the Taliban for the purpose of forced recruitment, but there is insufficient evidence to suggest that this is anything more that a mere possibility, and the Panel finds that there is not even a serious possibility that the minor would be persecuted for this or any other reason upon a hypothetical return to Afghanistan.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel found no convincing evidence that the claimants, including the female and minor, face more risk from the Taliban than other Afghans.

propositions.text: The Panel finds claimants are not Convention refugees under s. 96 nor persons in need of protection under s. 97 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: the Panel finds the claimants to not be Convention refugees under s. 96 nor persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Claims are rejected for all claimants for the reasons noted above.
propositions.quote: As such, for the reasons noted above, the claims are rejected with respect to all claimants.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel concludes the claimants are not refugees or protected persons and rejects their claims.
